\section{Benjamini-Hochberg FDR Correction}
\label{app:bh-fdr}

Table~\ref{tab:bh-fdr} compares Bonferroni ($k{=}4$, per model$\times$strategy family) and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across all 44 statistical tests. BH-FDR recovers 5 additional significant results beyond Bonferroni, all in low-effect-size conditions (random eviction or cross-training-paradigm random comparisons). All 32 Bonferroni-significant results remain significant under BH-FDR.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Bonferroni vs.\ BH-FDR correction summary ($\alpha{=}0.05$, 44 tests). ``BH only'' denotes tests significant under BH-FDR but not Bonferroni.}
\label{tab:bh-fdr}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
Category & Bonf.\ sig. & BH-only sig. \\
\midrule
Per-condition Wilcoxon ($k{=}16$) & 10 & 2 \\
Imp vs.\ rand ($k{=}8$) & 8 & 0 \\
Adjacent sparsity ($k{=}12$) & 10 & 1 \\
Cross-paradigm Mann-Whitney ($k{=}8$) & 4 & 2 \\
\midrule
Total ($k{=}44$) & 32 & 5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The 5 BH-only results are: DeepSeek random $s{=}0.25$ and $s{=}0.30$ per-condition Wilcoxon ($p_{\text{Bonf}}{=}0.064$/$0.065$, BH $q{=}0.002$), DeepSeek random $s{=}0.25 \to 0.30$ adjacent-sparsity step ($p_{\text{Bonf}}{=}0.078$, BH $q{=}0.002$), and cross-training-paradigm random $s{=}0.25$/$s{=}0.30$ Mann-Whitney ($p_{\text{Bonf}}{=}0.66$/$0.17$, BH $q{=}0.018$/$0.005$). All involve random eviction---the weakest effects---confirming that Bonferroni is conservative but does not miss any importance-based findings.


\section{Minimum Phase Length Sensitivity}
\label{app:mpl-sensitivity}

Table~\ref{tab:mpl-sensitivity} reports the paired median difference $\Delta$ under three \texttt{min\_phase\_length} (mpl) settings across all 16 conditions (2 models $\times$ 2 strategies $\times$ 4 sparsity levels). Conclusions are robust: all importance-based conditions remain significant at $p_{\text{Bonf}} < 10^{-10}$ across mpl $\in \{5, 10, 20\}$; random conditions maintain the same significance pattern (non-significant at $s \leq 0.20$, significant at $s \geq 0.25$). Median $\Delta$ values vary by $<5\%$ between mpl settings for DeepSeek importance, confirming that the severity gradient is not an artifact of the merging threshold.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Sensitivity of median $\Delta$ to \texttt{min\_phase\_length} (mpl). $n_{\text{eff}}$: effective sample size after exclusions. All importance-based $p_{\text{Bonf}} < 10^{-10}$; ``ns'' denotes $p_{\text{Bonf}} > 0.05$.}
\label{tab:mpl-sensitivity}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Model & Strategy & $s$ & \multicolumn{1}{c}{mpl$=$5} & \multicolumn{1}{c}{mpl$=$10} & \multicolumn{1}{c}{mpl$=$20} & $n_{\text{eff}}$(10) & $n_{\text{eff}}$(20) \\

\section{Segmentation Robustness}
\label{app:seg-robust}

Table~\ref{tab:seg-robust} reports the paired median difference $\Delta$ under tercile, quartile, and quintile segmentation for both models under importance-based eviction. The extreme mean/median ratio (up to $97{,}640{:}1$ in individual conditions) reflects heavy-tailed II distributions driven by near-zero denominators in specific problems. \paragraph{Compound compression.}
Combining multiple compression axes produces non-additive errors.
\cite{spark-aaai2026} report super-additive degradation when combining channel pruning with token eviction; \cite{slim-icml2025} formalize compound error for quantization and sparsity.
\cite{unicomp-2026} evaluate compound compression across 40+ benchmarks, revealing that reasoning capabilities degrade disproportionately.
\cite{phase-transition-compression-2026} characterize independent phase transition points per compression dimension, implying the joint safe region is the intersection of per-dimension safe zones.
GRASPrune~\cite{graspune-acl2026} learns global budget-constrained gates for joint pruning but treats decisions as static across generation.
PM-KVQ~\cite{pmkvq-iclr2026} demonstrates that progressive quantization---gradually reducing bit-width over the generation process---mitigates cumulative error in long-CoT reasoning, implicitly introducing a temporal dimension to compression severity that resonates with our finding that compound interaction is phase-dependent.

These works establish compound interaction but share an implicit assumption: interaction magnitude is constant across the generation process.

\paragraph{KV cache eviction.}
Most methods rely on importance scoring whose reliability is increasingly questioned.
Ada-KV~\cite{adakv-neurips2025} introduces per-head adaptive budgets; SnapKV~\cite{snapkv-neurips2024} compresses from a fixed observation window; \cite{defensivekv-iclr2026} show worst-case loss $2.3$--$4.3{\times}$ higher than expected under standard aggregation.
\cite{nacl-acl2024} combine proxy-token and random eviction to counter attention bias.
RetentiveKV~\cite{retentivekv-2026} identifies deferred importance, and \cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026} show that single importance metrics exhibit systematic greedy bias.
\cite{hies-2025} independently show that importance scores flatten under heavy single-axis pruning. Our work extends this to the compound setting, revealing that flattening is amplified by the interaction of two compression axes and modulated by reasoning phase---phenomena absent in single-axis analysis. The crossover effect (\S\ref{sec:crossover}) is a prediction that single-axis frameworks cannot generate.
RLKV~\cite{rlkv-2025} uses reinforcement learning to identify reasoning-critical heads and selectively preserve their KV caches, demonstrating that head-level importance varies significantly for reasoning tasks. LongFlow~\cite{longflow-2026} targets the long-output setting of reasoning models with an efficient importance metric derived from attention intermediates.
Lethe~\cite{lethe-aaai2026} introduces temporal adaptivity with layer-wise multi-round pruning, and SparK~\cite{spark-aaai2026} extends eviction to the channel dimension with recoverable sparsity.
MUSTAFAR~\cite{mustafar-neurips2025} applies multi-stage adaptive compression for reasoning, while LKV~\cite{lkv-2026} learns end-to-end head-wise budgets for KV cache allocation.
Concurrent work examines KV cache compression's impact on reasoning capabilities \citep{hold-onto-thought-neurips2025}, evaluating single-axis compression strategies on mathematical reasoning benchmarks; our work extends this analysis to the compound setting where head pruning and KV eviction interact.

These methods each optimize a single pruning axis---whether aggregation, metric, temporal, or channel---without characterizing compound interactions when multiple mechanisms are simultaneously active.

\paragraph{Phase-aware inference.}
ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} applies different KV strategies per phase but without compound interaction.
\cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} find pruning sensitivity depends on ``silent'' vs.\ ``decisive'' representation phases.
\cite{doing-more-with-less-2026} show pruning combined with test-time scaling can exceed unpruned baselines; \cite{sparse-frontier-2025} find no universally optimal sparse attention strategy across generation stages.
\cite{physics-kvcache-2026} identify a sharp phase transition in single-axis KV cache compression at high sparsity, characterizing the single-dimension failure mode that our compound analysis extends across multiple axes.
R-KV~\cite{rkv-neurips2025} exploits reasoning-specific redundancy for aggressive cache compression, targeting per-axis optimization rather than characterizing compound degradation.
These works establish phase-dependent compression tolerance along single axes.
Our work bridges this by quantifying how compound severity varies across phases and eviction strategies.

## ForesightKV Overview

ForesightKV is a training-based KV cache eviction framework that learns to predict which KV pairs to evict during long-text generations.

## Key Innovation: Learning Long-Term Contribution

ForesightKV learns to predict the long-term contribution of each KV pair and adaptively evicts less important ones during generation. More specifically, the key idea is to train a lightweight scoring model that estimates the dynamic importance of each KV pair and guides eviction decisions.

## Training Methodology

The framework employs a two-stage training approach:

1. First, a Golden Eviction algorithm identifies the optimal eviction KV pairs at each step using future attention scores, and these traces and scores are then distilled via supervised training with a Pairwise Ranking Loss.

2. Furthermore, cache eviction is formulated as a Markov Decision Process and the GRPO algorithm is applied to mitigate the significant language modeling loss increase on low-entropy tokens.

## Performance Results

Experiments on AIME2024 and AIME2025 benchmarks of three reasoning models demonstrate that ForesightKV consistently outperforms prior methods under only half the cache budget, while benefiting synergistically from both supervised and reinforcement learning approaches.

The paper was submitted to arXiv on February 3, 2026.

## ThinK: Thinner Key Cache by Query-Driven Pruning

ThinK is a novel query-dependent KV cache pruning method that effectively reduces memory costs by over 20% in long-context scenarios without compromising the accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs).

### Key Approach

Unlike existing approaches that optimize memory based on sequence length, ThinK identifies substantial redundancy in the channel dimension of the KV cache, as indicated by an uneven magnitude distribution and a low-rank structure in the attention weights.

ThinK is a novel query-dependent KV cache pruning method designed to minimize attention weight loss while selectively pruning the least significant channels.

### Compound Compression

The method can be combined with other compression techniques - for instance, it prunes 40% of the key cache channels, followed by quantization of the remaining channels into 2-bit, demonstrating effective compound compression when integrated with methods like KIVI.

Results demonstrate that combining methods like H2O or SnapKV with ThinK consistently outperforms their counterparts without ThinK while maintaining the same memory footprint, highlighting the effectiveness of integrating query-driven channel pruning with KV cache compression methods.

### Publication and Evaluation

The paper was authored by Yuhui Xu, Zhanming Jie, Hanze Dong, Lei Wang, Xudong Lu, Aojun Zhou, Amrita Saha, Caiming Xiong, and Doyen Sahoo, published on Arxiv 2024. Extensive evaluations on the LLaMA3 and Mistral models across various long-sequence datasets confirm the efficacy of ThinK.

## "Prune-then-Quantize or Quantize-then-Prune?" Research

A recent study addresses whether the order matters when multiple compression methods are combined, as joint model compression has emerged as a powerful strategy to achieve higher efficiency by combining multiple methods such as pruning and quantization.

### Key Findings

The compression order—or the sequence of different methods within the compression pipeline—is a central but underexplored factor in joint model compression, as most prior studies have either sidestepped the issue by assuming orthogonality between techniques or examined them only in highly constrained cases, leaving the broader role of compression order in shaping model performance poorly understood.

The research introduces the Progressive Intensity Hypothesis, which states that weaker perturbations should precede stronger ones. More specifically, neural networks compressed by multiple methods perform better when weaker perturbations are applied first and stronger ones later.

### Previous Work

One notable prior attempt presents a theoretical framework proving the non-orthogonality of pruning and quantization, concluding that pruning followed by quantization is always preferable, though the scope of the work remains narrow and less practical, focusing only on magnitude-based pruning and max-scaled quantization.

### Practical Recommendations

A common and effective workflow is to first prune a model, then quantize the result, and use knowledge distillation to fine-tune and recover any lost performance.

The paper appears to have been published in March 2026 (arXiv) and was presented at ICLR 2026, making it one of the most recent comprehensive analyses of compression order effects.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length \cite{kwon-sosp2023, pope-mlsys2023}.
Two complementary responses---\emph{attention head pruning} \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019} and \emph{KV cache eviction} \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}---can be deployed simultaneously as \emph{compound sparsity}, but the resulting quality degradation is often super-additive \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}. Recent evaluations confirm that reasoning capabilities degrade disproportionately under compound compression \cite{unicomp-2026}, and that per-dimension safe zones intersect to form a smaller joint safe region \cite{phase-transition-compression-2026}.

Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as roughly constant across generation \cite{spark-aaai2026, unicomp-2026}, despite evidence that pruning sensitivity depends on representational phase \cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} and that no single sparse attention strategy dominates across generation stages \cite{sparse-frontier-2025}.
This assumption is problematic for reasoning models, whose generations alternate between broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning) and sharply concentrated attention (structured computation) \cite{thinkv-iclr2026}.
Phase-aware methods like ThinKV \cite{thinkv-iclr2026} apply different KV strategies per phase but without considering compound interaction, while importance-based eviction itself faces challenges from greedy bias \cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026}, deferred importance \cite{retentivekv-2026}, and temporal dynamics in long generations \cite{lethe-aaai2026}. These methods each optimize a single pruning axis; we characterize the interaction when multiple mechanisms are composed.
If compound severity varies across these phases, a uniform sparsity budget may be safe in one phase yet destructive in another.

What does compound interaction add beyond single-axis findings? HIES~\cite{hies-2025} characterizes score collapse; ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} introduces phase-aware eviction; \citet{sparse-frontier-2025} document strategy non-dominance across stages. Combining these insights qualitatively predicts phase-dependent compound degradation---but two quantitative patterns cannot be derived from single-axis analyses. First, the severity gradient follows a \emph{strictly monotonic dose-response} across sparsity levels (Jonckheere-Terpstra $z{=}33.7$, $p \ll 10^{-10}$), not merely a directional trend. Second, in DeepSeek a \emph{strategy ranking crossover} emerges at $s{=}0.25$---importance-based eviction simultaneously outperforms random in high-sparsity phases and underperforms in low-sparsity phases; Qwen shows consistent importance dominance without crossover, indicating model dependence. We report both the paired median difference $\Delta$ ($0.39 \to 8.48$) as the primary metric and the amplification ratio $G{=}7.5$--$79.8{\times}$ (importance) vs.\ $G \approx 1$ (random) as an auxiliary measure; $G$ is amplified by near-zero $\mathrm{II}_{\textit{high}}$ denominators, but $\Delta$---which involves no ratios---shows the same monotonic gradient (\S\ref{sec:results}).

We show that compound sparsity severity is strongly modulated by reasoning phase and eviction strategy.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive degradation---concentrates in low-sparsity phases and is largely absent in high-sparsity phases.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (500 MATH-500 problems), the median phase difference rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $8.48$ at $s{=}0.30$ (all Bonferroni-corrected $p \ll 10^{-10}$; Jonckheere-Terpstra $z{=}33.7$, $p \ll 10^{-10}$).
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($\Delta$: $0.07 \to 3.16$; all $p < 10^{-14}$); preliminary evidence from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM) suggests the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2 but at ${\sim}1/40$ the magnitude and with substantially weaker strategy contrast.
Random eviction develops a detectable but weak phase gradient only above $s \approx 0.20$ ($3$--$17{\times}$ smaller than importance-based where both strategies are significant, $s \geq 0.25$), confirming that the dominant gradient is an emergent phase-strategy interaction.

We present preliminary correlational evidence for \emph{importance score flattening}---the degeneration of head importance scores toward uniformity under compound stress---as a contributing factor, with the \emph{structural specificity} of importance-based pruning (which selectively removes high-score heads) as a key differentiator from random pruning.

This work is a \textbf{diagnostic study}: we characterize a previously unknown interaction effect rather than proposing a mitigation method. Following the tradition of empirical analysis papers in NLP \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019}, our contribution is establishing and quantifying the phenomenon of phase-modulated compound severity, providing measurement tools and diagnostic findings that inform future method design.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify a \textbf{phase--strategy interaction}: importance-based eviction exhibits a severity gradient across reasoning phases that is $3$--$17{\times}$ larger than under random eviction where both strategies show significant phase gradients ($s \geq 0.25$; \S\ref{sec:results}).\footnote{The full range including non-significant random conditions ($s \leq 0.20$, where random $\Delta$ CIs span zero) extends to $39{\times}$.}
    \item We show this gradient \textbf{increases monotonically with sparsity} and replicates across two Qwen2-architecture models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), with exploratory evidence from a LlamaForCausalLM model suggesting the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2 (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We provide a \textbf{diagnostic analysis} revealing that aggregate score flattening (Gini) is necessary but not sufficient for severity amplification, pointing to structural specificity of pruned heads as the key differentiator (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}
Compound sparsity---simultaneously pruning attention heads and evicting KV cache entries---is essential for efficient LLM inference but produces super-additive quality degradation whose structure is poorly understood.
We show that compound severity is not phase-invariant: it is an emergent phase-strategy interaction with amplification ratios ($G$) from $7.5{\times}$ ($s{=}0.15$, 95\% CI $[4.1, 11.4]$) to $79.8{\times}$ ($s{=}0.30$, 95\% CI $[63.3, 96.5]$; additive null; multiplicative null yields larger estimates) across reasoning phases in mathematical reasoning models.

On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (500 MATH-500 problems, $n_{\text{eff}}{=}496$, $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$), importance-based eviction produces a monotonically increasing severity gradient from the high-sparsity to low-sparsity reasoning phase (median $\Delta$: $0.39 \to 8.48$; all Bonferroni-corrected $p \ll 10^{-10}$). Random eviction develops a detectable phase gradient only above $s \approx 0.20$ (non-significant at $s \leq 0.20$; where significant, $3$--$17{\times}$ weaker), confirming importance-based eviction as the dominant driver.
A crossover emerges at $s{=}0.25$: importance-based eviction outperforms random in high-sparsity phases yet underperforms in low-sparsity phases---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($n_{\text{eff}}{=}475$, $\Delta$: $0.07 \to 3.16$; all $p < 10^{-14}$), with preliminary cross-architecture evidence from a LlamaForCausalLM model suggesting the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2-family architectures.
We present \emph{importance score flattening}---the degeneration of head importance scores toward uniformity under compound stress---as a correlational diagnostic: both strategies exhibit near-identical Gini drops, yet severity diverges by $15$--$17{\times}$, implicating the structural specificity of importance-based pruning as the key differentiator.
These findings establish the phase-dependent nature of compound severity as a diagnostic foundation for future phase-aware mitigation strategies.
\end{abstract}

4	The mechanisms discussed here are \emph{correlational diagnostics} that illuminate but do not fully explain the $15$--$17{\times}$ severity divergence between strategies. Both strategies exhibit near-identical Gini drops ($<10\%$ difference), yet severity diverges by $15$--$17{\times}$, indicating that aggregate concentration collapse alone is insufficient. The critical differentiator is \emph{structural specificity} of importance-based pruning, which systematically removes high-attention-score heads (\S\ref{sec:discrimination-collapse-main}).

7	\label{sec:discrimination-collapse-main}
8	
9	Head pruning systematically reduces the discriminative power of cumulative importance scores, suggesting a mechanism for the phase-strategy interaction. The Gini coefficient decreases by $0.030$--$0.081$ (DeepSeek, $6$--$17\%$ relative to dense baseline) and $0.010$--$0.020$ (Qwen, $2$--$4\%$) after pruning, with consistent negative deltas in all 16 conditions (Appendix~\ref{app:analysis}, Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics-full}). Critically, random eviction shows near-identical Gini drops at matched sparsity (DeepSeek $s{=}0.25$: importance $-0.065$ vs.\ random $-0.060$; $s{=}0.30$: $-0.081$ vs.\ $-0.071$; Qwen: $-0.019$ to $-0.046$ for both strategies), confirming that importance score flattening is a consequence of head pruning \emph{per se}, not the eviction strategy. Yet importance-based severity is $15$--$17{\times}$ larger than random at matched sparsity---the amplification arises because importance-based eviction \emph{depends on} the very scores that pruning degrades, while random eviction's decisions are score-independent.
10	
11	This pattern---\emph{importance score flattening}---is consistent with importance-based eviction degenerating into noise-sensitive selection when score distributions flatten. The effect is phase-dependent: in low-sparsity phases, attention is already broadly distributed, so pruning-induced flattening has maximum impact; in high-sparsity phases, concentration is preserved. This observation is independently corroborated by \cite{hies-2025}, who report importance score collapse under heavy single-axis pruning; our results extend this to the compound setting, where flattening is amplified by the interaction of two compression axes and modulated by reasoning phase.
12	
13	To provide quantitative evidence for structural specificity, we analyzed the attention Gini coefficients of importance-pruned versus retained heads. Importance pruning (Frobenius norm criterion) systematically removes heads with lower Gini coefficients---i.e., heads with more dispersed attention patterns (Mann-Whitney $U$, $p < 10^{-28}$; rank-biserial $r = 0.62$--$0.76$ across all 8 conditions). Random pruning, by contrast, samples heads with Gini indistinguishable from the population mean (200-trial verification). We acknowledge that the Frobenius norm and Gini coefficient share sensitivity to attention weight magnitude, making their correlation partially expected; the key evidence is the consistent large effect size ($r > 0.6$) indicating strong structural separation between pruned and retained head sets.
14	
15	We note that this evidence is correlational; causal validation through controlled manipulation of importance-score entropy is an important direction for future work.

18	\label{sec:entropy-redistribution-main}

\begin{abstract}
Compound sparsity---simultaneously pruning attention heads and evicting KV cache entries---is essential for efficient LLM inference but produces super-additive quality degradation whose structure is poorly understood.
We show that compound severity is not phase-invariant: it is an emergent phase-strategy interaction with amplification ratios ($G$) from $7.5{\times}$ ($s{=}0.15$, 95\% CI $[4.1, 11.4]$) to $79.8{\times}$ ($s{=}0.30$, 95\% CI $[63.3, 96.5]$; additive null; multiplicative null yields larger estimates) across reasoning phases in mathematical reasoning models.

On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (500 MATH-500 problems, $n_{\text{eff}}{=}496$, $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$), importance-based eviction produces a monotonically increasing severity gradient from the high-sparsity to low-sparsity reasoning phase (median $\Delta$: $0.39 \to 8.48$; all Bonferroni-corrected $p \ll 10^{-10}$). Random eviction develops a detectable phase gradient only above $s \approx 0.20$ (non-significant at $s \leq 0.20$; where significant, $3$--$17{\times}$ weaker), confirming importance-based eviction as the dominant driver.
A crossover emerges at $s{=}0.25$: importance-based eviction outperforms random in high-sparsity phases yet underperforms in low-sparsity phases---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($n_{\text{eff}}{=}475$, $\Delta$: $0.07 \to 3.16$; all $p < 10^{-14}$), with preliminary cross-architecture evidence from a LlamaForCausalLM model suggesting the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2-family architectures.
We present \emph{importance score flattening}---the degeneration of head importance scores toward uniformity under compound stress---as a correlational diagnostic: both strategies exhibit near-identical Gini drops, yet severity diverges by $15$--$17{\times}$, implicating the structural specificity of importance-based pruning as the key differentiator.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length \cite{kwon-sosp2023, pope-mlsys2023}.
Two complementary responses---\emph{attention head pruning} \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019} and \emph{KV cache eviction} \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}---can be deployed simultaneously as \emph{compound sparsity}, but the resulting quality degradation is often super-additive \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}. Recent evaluations confirm that reasoning capabilities degrade disproportionately under compound compression \cite{unicomp-2026}, and that per-dimension safe zones intersect to form a smaller joint safe region \cite{phase-transition-compression-2026}.

Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as roughly constant across generation \cite{spark-aaai2026, unicomp-2026}, despite evidence that pruning sensitivity depends on representational phase \cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} and that no single sparse attention strategy dominates across generation stages \cite{sparse-frontier-2025}.
This assumption is problematic for reasoning models, whose generations alternate between broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning) and sharply concentrated attention (structured computation) \cite{thinkv-iclr2026}.
Phase-aware methods like ThinKV \cite{thinkv-iclr2026} apply different KV strategies per phase but without considering compound interaction, while importance-based eviction itself faces challenges from greedy bias \cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026}, deferred importance \cite{retentivekv-2026}, and temporal dynamics in long generations \cite{lethe-aaai2026}. These methods each optimize a single pruning axis; we characterize the interaction when multiple mechanisms are composed.
If compound severity varies across these phases, a uniform sparsity budget may be safe in one phase yet destructive in another.

What does compound interaction add beyond single-axis findings? HIES~\cite{hies-2025} characterizes score collapse; ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} introduces phase-aware eviction; \citet{sparse-frontier-2025} document strategy non-dominance across stages. Combining these insights qualitatively predicts phase-dependent compound degradation---but two quantitative patterns cannot be derived from single-axis analyses. First, the severity gradient follows a \emph{strictly monotonic dose-response} across sparsity levels (Jonckheere-Terpstra $z{=}33.7$, $p \ll 10^{-10}$), not merely a directional trend. Second, in DeepSeek a \emph{strategy ranking crossover} emerges at $s{=}0.25$---importance-based eviction simultaneously outperforms random in high-sparsity phases and underperforms in low-sparsity phases; Qwen shows consistent importance dominance without crossover, indicating model dependence. We report both the paired median difference $\Delta$ ($0.39 \to 8.48$) as the primary metric and the amplification ratio $G{=}7.5$--$79.8{\times}$ (importance) vs.\ $G \approx 1$ (random) as an auxiliary measure; $G$ is amplified by near-zero $\mathrm{II}_{\textit{high}}$ denominators, but $\Delta$---which involves no ratios---shows the same monotonic gradient (\S\ref{sec:results}).

We show that compound sparsity severity is strongly modulated by reasoning phase and eviction strategy.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive degradation---concentrates in low-sparsity phases and is largely absent in high-sparsity phases.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (500 MATH-500 problems), the median phase difference rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $8.48$ at $s{=}0.30$ (all Bonferroni-corrected $p \ll 10^{-10}$; Jonckheere-Terpstra $z{=}33.7$, $p \ll 10^{-10}$).
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($\Delta$: $0.07 \to 3.16$; all $p < 10^{-14}$); preliminary evidence from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM) suggests the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2 but at ${\sim}1/40$ the magnitude and with substantially weaker strategy contrast.
Random eviction develops a detectable but weak phase gradient only above $s \approx 0.20$ ($3$--$17{\times}$ smaller than importance-based where both strategies are significant, $s \geq 0.25$), confirming that the dominant gradient is an emergent phase-strategy interaction.

We present preliminary correlational evidence for \emph{importance score flattening}---the degeneration of head importance scores toward uniformity under compound stress---as a contributing factor, with the \emph{structural specificity} of importance-based pruning (which selectively removes high-score heads) as a key differentiator from random pruning.

This work is a \textbf{diagnostic study}: we characterize a previously unknown interaction effect rather than proposing a mitigation method. Following the tradition of empirical analysis papers in NLP \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019}, our contribution is establishing and quantifying the phenomenon of phase-modulated compound severity, providing measurement tools and diagnostic findings that inform future method design.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify a \textbf{phase--strategy interaction}: importance-based eviction exhibits a severity gradient across reasoning phases that is $3$--$17{\times}$ larger than under random eviction where both strategies show significant phase gradients ($s \geq 0.25$; \S\ref{sec:results}).\footnote{The full range including non-significant random conditions ($s \leq 0.20$, where random $\Delta$ CIs span zero) extends to $39{\times}$.}
    \item We show this gradient \textbf{increases monotonically with sparsity} and replicates across two Qwen2-architecture models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), with exploratory evidence from a LlamaForCausalLM model suggesting the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2 (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We provide a \textbf{diagnostic analysis} revealing that aggregate score flattening (Gini) is necessary but not sufficient for severity amplification, pointing to structural specificity of pruned heads as the key differentiator (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}
